q: Why do you resample every call to 16 kHz mono rather than keeping the native 8 kHz telephony rate?
a: The three SSL deepfake pipelines (wav2vec2-base, XLS-R, DistilHuBERT) were all pretrained on 16 kHz audio, so load_audio resamples to 16 kHz mono to match their front-end feature extraction. Keeping 8 kHz would fold the top octave and force the models off-distribution. Note 8 kHz is never a resample target for us: it is instead a DETECTED channel flag raised when hf_energy_ratio < 0.02, which then switches us to the narrowband threshold set.

q: G.711 at 8 kHz gives you a 4 kHz Nyquist, yet you say vocoder artifacts live above 6 kHz. How can your detector work on a phone call?
a: It largely cannot rely on the >6 kHz cue on a true 8 kHz G.711 leg — that band is gone, which is exactly why G.711 8k degrades EER to 15.0% (+7.5 pts vs 7.5% clean). We compensate by detecting the narrowband channel (hf_energy_ratio < 0.02) and raising thresholds (HIGH 0.85 / MED 0.55) so the missing HF band does not inflate false positives, and we lean on the SSL embeddings and prosody cues that survive band-limiting rather than on raw HF energy.

q: Contrast LFCC, MFCC and CQCC. Why does VoxShield use LFCC and CQCC in its 89-dim bank rather than plain MFCC?
a: MFCC applies a mel filterbank that compresses high-frequency resolution, which is where vocoder artifacts sit, so it is suboptimal for spoof detection. LFCC uses a linear filterbank giving uniform resolution across frequency, preserving HF detail; CQCC is derived from the Constant-Q Transform (84 bins here) whose geometrically-spaced bins give high frequency resolution at low frequencies and high time resolution at high frequencies. VoxShield uses LFCC 40 (n_lfcc=20, mean+std) + CQCC 40 (CQT 84 bins → DCT → mean+std), the classic ASVspoof-proven anti-spoofing pair, and omits MFCC deliberately.

q: Why apply a DCT after the log filterbank / CQT at all?
a: The DCT decorrelates the log-spectral coefficients and compacts energy into the low-order cepstral coefficients, so keeping n_lfcc=20 (or the CQCC low quefrencies) captures the spectral envelope while discarding fine pitch harmonics. Decorrelation matters because our downstream head is a diagonal-ish logistic model where correlated inputs would distort weights, and truncation gives a compact, fixed-length descriptor we can take mean+std over frames.

q: What does the CQT buy you over an STFT for detecting synthetic speech?
a: The Constant-Q Transform spaces its bins geometrically (constant ratio of center frequency to bandwidth), matching musical/harmonic structure and giving finer frequency resolution in the low bands where pitch and formants live, and finer time resolution up high. We use 84 CQT bins → DCT → CQCC (40 dims, mean+std). This resolves harmonic regularity that TTS vocoders often over-smooth, complementing the linear LFCC view.

q: Explain the group-delay / phase feature. Why does phase matter for deepfake detection when humans are near phase-deaf?
a: Many vocoders and TTS systems reconstruct or ignore phase (e.g., Griffin-Lim, or neural vocoders with imperfect phase modeling), leaving unnatural group-delay structure even when the magnitude spectrum looks natural. We capture this as phase_reg, a group-delay proxy scalar in the 9-dim block. Human insensitivity to phase is irrelevant to a machine detector: the phase residue is a discriminative fingerprint of the synthesis pipeline, not a perceptual cue.

q: Walk through the prosody scalars. How are F0 jitter and shimmer computed and why do they flag clones?
a: We derive f0 via pyin, then compute f0_jitter (cycle-to-cycle F0 perturbation), shimmer (cycle-to-cycle amplitude perturbation), and f0_voiced_ratio. Natural voiced speech carries small stochastic jitter/shimmer from biological glottal variation; many TTS systems produce F0 contours that are either too smooth (under-jittered) or unnaturally regular. These three scalars sit in the 9-dim block and feed both the DSP heuristic and the 89-dim head.

q: Why is hf_energy_ratio (>6 kHz band energy) such a load-bearing feature, and what is its failure mode?
a: Neural vocoders frequently under-generate or over-regularize energy above ~6 kHz, so hf_energy_ratio and hf_regularity are strong cues on wideband audio. The failure mode is band-limited channels: on 8 kHz telephony the >6 kHz band is physically absent, so hf_energy_ratio < 0.02 no longer indicates a fake — it indicates narrowband. That is precisely why we treat low HF energy as a channel flag and switch thresholds rather than as evidence of synthesis.

q: Define spectral flatness and explain its role here.
a: Spectral flatness is the ratio of the geometric mean to the arithmetic mean of the power spectrum (a value near 1 is noise-like/flat, near 0 is tonal/peaky). It is one of the 9 scalars, used to characterize how noise-like versus harmonically-structured a frame is; over-smoothed synthetic speech and certain vocoder noise floors shift flatness away from natural distributions. It complements hf_regularity in describing spectral texture.

q: Why do you drop silence before feature extraction, and what artifact could that introduce?
a: We drop silence with librosa.effects.split(top_db=30) so that features and SSL embeddings are computed over actual speech, not over channel noise or dead air that would dilute the mean/std statistics and waste the 6 s speech cap. The risk is that aggressive silence removal can concatenate segments and distort prosody/breath cues, so we retain silence_ratio and breath_score as scalars — the removed silence is still summarized rather than fully discarded.

q: You cap analysis at the first 6 seconds of speech. Justify this against information loss.
a: After silence removal we cap at the first 6 s of speech to bound latency and memory and to give the SSL models a consistent, batch-free input length; empirically the discriminative spectral/prosodic fingerprint is present in the first few seconds. The cost is that evidence later in a long clip is ignored by the clip detector — which is exactly why the streaming path exists, sliding a 3 s window with 1 s hop across the whole call and accumulating evidence rather than truncating.

q: What is RawBoost / codec augmentation and how does it relate to your robustness profile?
a: RawBoost-style and codec augmentation inject convolutive/impulsive noise and re-encode audio through telephony codecs during training so the model sees channel-degraded spoofs. Our deployed model is codec-hardened, which shows in the results: Opus 12k actually IMPROVES EER to 2.5% (−5.0 pts) and the model tolerates G.711/MP3 far better than benign DSP. The honest gap is that we did NOT match-augment pitch/tempo/noise, so those still degrade heavily (+25 to +49 pts).

q: Why does the DSP acoustic detector combine hf, phase, prosody and breath with those specific weights (0.34/0.24/0.24/0.18)?
a: The acoustic-dsp detector is a pure hand-tuned heuristic: fake_prob = 0.34·hf + 0.24·phase + 0.24·prosody + 0.18·breath, weighting the high-frequency vocoder cue most, phase and prosody equally, and breath least. It is deliberately transparent and model-free so it degrades gracefully and is interpretable, but it is the weakest single detector (47.4% EER / 0.521 AUC). Its value is as a diverse, uncorrelated input to the stacker, not as a standalone classifier — reflected in its small negative stacker weight.

q: What is breath_score and why include it?
a: breath_score is one of the 9 scalars, quantifying the presence and character of breath/aspiration noise between phrases. Genuine speakers produce inhalation and aspiration artifacts that many TTS systems omit or render unnaturally, so its absence or abnormal regularity is a weak clone cue. It carries the smallest weight (0.18) in the DSP heuristic, acknowledging it is a soft, easily-spoofed signal.

q: Your feature vector is exactly 89 dimensions. Decompose it and explain why fixed-length matters.
a: 89 = LFCC 40 (n_lfcc=20 × mean+std) + CQCC 40 (CQT 84 bins → DCT, mean+std) + 9 scalars (hf_energy_ratio, hf_regularity, spectral_flatness, phase_reg, f0_jitter, shimmer, f0_voiced_ratio, silence_ratio, breath_score). The mean+std pooling over frames collapses a variable-length clip into a fixed 89-vector so the logistic head and closed-form SHAP operate on a constant feature space regardless of clip duration.

q: Explain the wav2vec2 architecture and why an SSL model beats a hand-crafted feature detector at spoof detection.
a: wav2vec2 has a convolutional feature encoder that turns raw waveform into latent frames, followed by a Transformer that contextualizes them; it is pretrained self-supervised via a contrastive masked-prediction objective on large unlabeled speech, learning rich acoustic representations. Those representations capture subtle synthesis artifacts that hand-crafted LFCC/CQCC miss, which is why XLS-R (a large multilingual wav2vec2) is our best single detector at 16.0% EER / 0.901 AUC versus 26.6% for the LFCC+CQCC head.

q: Distinguish wav2vec2, XLS-R and HuBERT. Why field all three rather than the single best one?
a: wav2vec2 uses contrastive masked prediction; XLS-R is wav2vec2-large scaled to 128 languages (cross-lingual); HuBERT (here DistilHuBERT, a distilled variant) uses offline-clustered hidden units as masked-prediction targets. We field all three because they learn from different objectives, data and capacities, so their errors are partially decorrelated — the stacker exploits that diversity. XLS-R (16.0%) and DistilHuBERT (24.9%) contribute strongly; the wav2vec2-base Deepfake-V2 is weak alone (62.0%) but still adds signal via a negative weight.

q: Why are the three HF models used frozen (no fine-tuning) in the deployed pipeline?
a: The deployed classifiers are used as-is via transformers.pipeline('audio-classification', model=ID) — we do not fine-tune them in production; the learning happens in the lightweight logistic stacker on top. Freezing keeps the heavy SSL backbones fixed and cheap to serve on CPU, avoids overfitting our small n_train=480 held-out split, and makes the system reproducible. We do have a fine-tuned xlsr_antispoof (1.18 GB) locally, but it is gitignored, not baked into Docker, and remains a roadmap asset rather than deployed.

q: What is the self-attention mechanism the Transformers in these models rely on?
a: Self-attention computes, for each frame, softmax(QKᵀ/√d)·V, letting every frame attend to every other frame so the model builds context-dependent representations (e.g., relating a vocoder artifact to its harmonic context). Multi-head attention runs several such projections in parallel to capture different relations. This is what lets wav2vec2/XLS-R/HuBERT model long-range acoustic dependencies that frame-local cepstral features cannot.

q: The LFCC+CQCC head is a LogisticRegressionNP over 89 dims with b=−0.512. Why does its name understate what it actually consumes?
a: The name 'LFCC+CQCC head' is just a label — the model is actually LogisticRegressionNP(89) operating over the FULL 89-dim vector, including the 9 scalars, not only the 80 cepstral dims. So it already fuses cepstral and prosodic/spectral evidence in one linear model with bias b=−0.512. It scores 26.6% EER / 0.786 AUC alone and gets a large positive stacker weight (+2.10) because it is a competent, decorrelated learner.

q: Why use ECAPA-TDNN for speaker verification and what is the 192-D embedding?
a: ECAPA-TDNN (speechbrain/spkrec-ecapa-voxceleb) is a time-delay net with squeeze-excitation and channel attention plus attentive statistics pooling that produces a 192-D speaker embedding, state-of-the-art on VoxCeleb. We compare enrolled vs incoming embeddings by cosine similarity against a verify threshold of 0.18 on CPU, yielding VERIFIED / REJECTED-CLONE / REJECTED-IDENTITY. Enrollment is in-memory only, so it is a demo-grade store, not persisted.

q: How does speaker verification (ECAPA) relate to deepfake detection (the 5-detector stack)? Aren't they solving different problems?
a: Yes — the 5-detector stack answers 'is this audio synthetic?' (spoof detection), while ECAPA answers 'is this the claimed speaker?' (identity). They are complementary: a clone that perfectly matches a target's identity could pass naive ASR but should be caught either by the spoof stack (synthesis artifacts) or, if enrolled, by ECAPA rejecting it as REJECTED-CLONE. Together they cover both 'fake voice' and 'wrong/impersonated voice' threats.

q: Why is Silero VAD gated before Whisper in the liveness challenge, and what failure does it prevent?
a: Whisper is prone to hallucinating tokens on silence or noise, so a Silero VAD gate runs first and only passes segments containing actual speech to Whisper. In the digit-challenge liveness flow this prevents Whisper from inventing spoken digits when the caller is silent, which would otherwise let an attacker (or dead air) spuriously 'pass' the challenge. We also cap decoding at max_new_tokens=32 to bound cost and hallucination.

q: You run three different Whisper configurations. Enumerate them and justify the differences.
a: Liveness/digit ASR uses transformers Whisper base.en with a tiny.en fallback (English digits, low latency, VAD-gated). Multilingual scam ASR uses openai-whisper 'small' because 'base' mis-decodes Hindi as Urdu. Language-ID for Indic routing uses openai-whisper 'base'. Each task trades accuracy vs latency differently, so the model size is chosen per task rather than one-size-fits-all.

q: Why prefer stacking over soft voting, hard voting, or simple averaging for fusing your five detectors?
a: The detectors are wildly unequal (XLS-R 16.0% EER vs Deepfake-V2 62.0%) and partially correlated, so unweighted schemes let weak/redundant learners drag the result — simple-average fusion scores 19.1% EER, worse than XLS-R alone. A learned logistic stacker assigns per-detector weights (even negative ones) and a bias fit on held-out data, driving the fused EER to 5.9%. Stacking learns how to trust each base model conditionally; voting/averaging cannot.

q: Simple-average fusion (19.1%) is worse than your single best detector (XLS-R 16.0%). Explain that inversion.
a: Averaging weights all five detectors equally, so the three weak learners (LFCC+CQCC head 26.6%, Acoustic-DSP 47.4%, Deepfake-V2 62.0%) collectively pull the mean toward noise and can overwhelm the two strong ones. Because Deepfake-V2 is anti-correlated with the truth (0.356 AUC, below 0.5), averaging it in without a sign flip actively hurts. The stacker fixes exactly this by learning a negative weight on Deepfake-V2 and small/negative weights on the weak DSP, recovering the strong learners' signal — 5.9% vs 19.1%.

q: The Deepfake-V2 detector has AUC 0.356 (below 0.5). Why keep a worse-than-random detector at all?
a: AUC 0.356 means it is systematically anti-correlated with ground truth, so it carries usable information once its sign is flipped. The stacker does exactly that with weight w=−1.17: subtracting its score adds discriminative signal. Discarding it would throw away that inverse evidence; keeping it with a negative weight is strictly better, which is why a learned stacker dominates naive averaging that could only add it positively.

q: Interpret the negative stacker weights −0.55 (acoustic-dsp) and −1.17 (Deepfake-V2) precisely.
a: In the standardized logit L = b + Σ wᵢ·zᵢ, a negative weight means higher detector output pushes the fused score toward GENUINE, not fake. For Deepfake-V2 (w=−1.17) this reflects its below-0.5 AUC — its 'fake' vote is evidence of genuine, so we invert it. For acoustic-dsp (w=−0.55) the heuristic is weak and partially redundant with better learners, so the stacker gives it a mild corrective negative role rather than trusting its fake votes.

q: Derive the logistic-regression prediction, log-loss, and gradient your stacker is trained with.
a: Prediction: p = sigmoid(w·x + b) = 1/(1+e^−(w·x+b)). Log-loss for label y∈{0,1}: L = −[y·ln p + (1−y)·ln(1−p)]. Its gradient is elegantly ∂L/∂w = (p − y)·x and ∂L/∂b = (p − y), so weights move proportionally to the prediction error times the input. Standardizing inputs (z=(x−μ)/sd) makes this gradient well-conditioned so the five weights converge stably.

q: Why standardize the detector outputs before the logistic stacker, and where do μ and sd come from?
a: Standardization z = (x−μ)/sd puts every detector on a common scale so one detector's larger numeric range doesn't dominate the weights, and it conditions the log-loss gradient (p−y)·z for stable convergence. μ and sd are per-detector statistics estimated on the training split. This same standardization is what makes the closed-form SHAP φᵢ=(wᵢ/sdᵢ)(xᵢ−μᵢ) exact, since the sd appears explicitly in the logit contribution.

q: Derive the closed-form SHAP φᵢ = (wᵢ/sdᵢ)(xᵢ − μᵢ) for the logistic head.
a: The logit is L(x) = b + Σ wᵢ·(xᵢ−μᵢ)/sdᵢ. For a linear/logistic model the exact Shapley value of feature i in logit space is its additive term relative to the baseline (all features at their mean): φᵢ = (wᵢ/sdᵢ)(xᵢ−μᵢ), because at x=μ every term is zero. By construction Σᵢ φᵢ = L(x) − L(μ) = final_logit − base_logit, so contributions sum exactly to the model output with no sampling and no `shap` dependency.

q: Why is closed-form SHAP exact here when SHAP is normally an approximation?
a: KernelSHAP/sampling approximations are needed for nonlinear or interacting models where marginal contributions depend on feature ordering. A logistic model is additive in logit space, so feature contributions do not interact — the Shapley value collapses to the single linear term (wᵢ/sdᵢ)(xᵢ−μᵢ). There is nothing to sample or approximate, and the exactness is provable by Σφᵢ = final_logit − base_logit.

q: Explain Platt calibration, derive it, and reconcile with your ECE actually rising after calibration.
a: Platt scaling fits p_cal = sigmoid(a·s + b) on the raw stacker score s via maximum likelihood; our fitted parameters are {a:6.446, b:−3.151}. It is meant to map scores to well-calibrated probabilities. Honestly, it did not help our ECE: uncalibrated ECE was 0.031 and calibrated is 0.044, so calibration slightly worsened it here — likely because the raw scores were already near-calibrated on n=320 and Platt overfit the small validation set. We report the calibrated number (0.044) transparently rather than cherry-picking.

q: Define EER and explain why you report it as the headline metric.
a: Equal Error Rate is the operating point where false-accept rate equals false-reject rate (FAR=FRR); a single threshold-independent scalar summarizing the ROC. We headline it (5.9%) because it is standard in anti-spoofing (ASVspoof) and avoids cherry-picking a favorable threshold. We still also report operating-point metrics at threshold 0.70 (accuracy 93.4%, precision 93.5%, recall 92.9%) because deployment runs at a fixed threshold, not at EER.

q: Define min t-DCF and why it matters more than accuracy for anti-spoofing.
a: The tandem Detection Cost Function weights spoof-detection errors by their downstream cost in a combined ASV+countermeasure system, using priors and cost coefficients rather than treating false-accepts and false-rejects symmetrically. min t-DCF (ours 0.252) is the minimum achievable cost over thresholds. It matters because in fraud the cost of accepting a clone (letting a fraudster through) differs from rejecting a genuine customer — accuracy hides that asymmetry.

q: Define ECE precisely and give its formula as you compute it.
a: Expected Calibration Error bins predictions by confidence and measures the gap between accuracy and confidence per bin, weighted by bin population: ECE = Σᵦ (nᵦ/N)·|acc(b) − conf(b)|. Ours is 0.044 calibrated (0.031 uncalibrated) at threshold 0.70. A low ECE means the predicted probability matches the empirical frequency of being correct, which matters when an analyst reads '0.8 fake' as an 80% likelihood.

q: Define the Brier score and how it differs from ECE.
a: The Brier score is the mean squared error between predicted probability and the 0/1 outcome: Brier = (1/N)·Σ (pᵢ − yᵢ)²; ours is 0.048. Unlike ECE (which only measures calibration via binning), Brier is a proper scoring rule decomposable into calibration + refinement (sharpness), so it penalizes both miscalibration and lack of discrimination in one number.

q: Distinguish ROC-AUC from PR-AUC. Given class balance ~50/50 here, which is more informative and why?
a: ROC plots TPR vs FPR and AUC is threshold-independent ranking quality; PR plots precision vs recall and is more sensitive under heavy class imbalance because it ignores true negatives. Our held-out set is near-balanced (144+11 fake vs 155+10 genuine at threshold 0.70, ~50/50), so ROC-AUC (0.983) is a fair and informative summary. In real deployment where genuine calls vastly outnumber fakes, PR-AUC would become the more honest metric.

q: Explain the recall-floor gate and why it is a deliberate, safe override of the calibrated probability.
a: The gate says: if max(distilhubert, xlsr) ≥ 0.90 AND the LFCC/CQCC head ≥ 0.5, floor the fused score to ≥ 0.70 (the HIGH threshold). It exists because when the two strongest, most-trusted detectors are both highly confident it is fake, we do not want the stacker's negative-weighted detectors to pull the fused score below the flag line. It trades a little precision for recall on high-confidence spoofs, which is the correct asymmetry for fraud — and it requires two independent strong votes to fire, limiting false triggers.

q: Write out the full stacker equation with the real weights and bias, and identify the sign of each contribution.
a: final_logit = b + w_dsp·z_dsp + w_dfv2·z_dfv2 + w_xlsr·z_xlsr + w_dhub·z_dhub + w_head·z_head = 0.134 + (−0.55)·z_dsp + (−1.17)·z_dfv2 + (1.21)·z_xlsr + (2.22)·z_dhub + (2.10)·z_head, then p = Platt(sigmoid(final_logit)) with {a:6.446,b:−3.151}. DistilHuBERT (+2.22) and the LFCC+CQCC head (+2.10) dominate positively, XLS-R (+1.21) adds, while Deepfake-V2 (−1.17) and acoustic-DSP (−0.55) are inverted/corrective.

q: Why is DistilHuBERT's stacker weight (+2.22) larger than XLS-R's (+1.21) even though XLS-R is the better single detector (16.0% vs 24.9%)?
a: Stacker weights reflect marginal, conditional value given the other detectors, not standalone accuracy. XLS-R and DistilHuBERT are both wav2vec2/HuBERT-family and partially correlated, so once XLS-R is in the model, some of its signal is redundant; DistilHuBERT apparently contributes more decorrelated residual information plus the LFCC+CQCC head overlaps XLS-R too. Standardization also rescales inputs, so weight magnitude is not directly comparable to single-detector EER.

q: How would you audit whether the learned stacker is overfitting five weights to n_train=480?
a: Five weights plus a bias on 480 training points is a low-variance fit, but I would still cross-validate the EER across folds, check weight stability under bootstrap resampling, and confirm the held-out n=320 EER (5.9%) tracks training EER without a large gap. The near-random-to-strong spread of base detectors and the fact that fused (5.9%) beats the best single (16.0%) by a wide margin argues against mere memorization. I would also verify the negative weights are stable in sign across folds, since a flipping sign would signal overfit.

q: In logit space, what threshold on the calibrated probability corresponds to 0.70, and how does Platt {a:6.446,b:−3.151} shape the curve?
a: p_cal = sigmoid(6.446·s − 3.151), so p_cal = 0.70 when 6.446·s − 3.151 = ln(0.7/0.3) ≈ 0.847, giving raw s ≈ 0.620. The large slope a=6.446 sharpens the mapping (small changes in raw score s swing probability quickly), and b=−3.151 shifts the 0.5 crossover to s ≈ 0.489. This is why the deployed threshold operates on p_cal rather than raw s, and why calibration parameters must be reported for reproducibility.

q: Your calibration did not improve ECE. Why keep Platt scaling at all rather than reverting to raw scores?
a: Even though ECE rose marginally (0.031 → 0.044), Platt scaling maps the raw stacker score onto a stable, monotonic probability scale with fixed {a,b}, which gives analysts a consistent 0–1 confidence and lets the fixed 0.70/0.85 thresholds have a probabilistic meaning across channels. The honest position is that calibration's benefit here is interpretability and consistency, not a lower ECE — and we report both numbers so no one is misled.

q: Derive why the sigmoid is the right link function for binary spoof/genuine and connect it to log-odds.
a: If we model log-odds linearly, ln(p/(1−p)) = w·x+b, solving for p gives p = 1/(1+e^−(w·x+b)) = sigmoid(w·x+b). So the sigmoid is not arbitrary: it is the inverse-logit that makes a linear model of log-odds. This is why each stacker weight wᵢ is interpretable as the additive change in log-odds of 'fake' per standardized unit of detector i, and why SHAP contributions live naturally in logit space.

q: The confusion matrix at 0.70 is TP144/TN155/FP10/FN11. Reconstruct precision, recall, and accuracy from it.
a: Precision = TP/(TP+FP) = 144/154 = 93.5%; Recall = TP/(TP+FN) = 144/155 = 92.9%; Accuracy = (TP+TN)/N = (144+155)/320 = 299/320 = 93.4%; F1 = 2·P·R/(P+R) ≈ 0.93. These match the reported operating-point metrics and total to n_test=320, confirming the numbers are internally consistent at the 0.70 threshold.

q: Why choose 0.70 as the wideband HIGH threshold rather than the EER-optimal point?
a: The EER point balances FAR and FRR equally, but for fraud we deliberately shade toward catching fakes while keeping genuine-customer friction acceptable, and 0.70 gives a concrete operating point (FP 10, FN 11 on 320) that maps cleanly through Platt calibration to a probability. It also anchors the recall-floor gate. Critically, HIGH never auto-blocks — it triggers human step-up — so the threshold is tuned for a review-triggering point, not an automated deny.

q: Why is the narrowband HIGH threshold raised to 0.85 instead of 0.70?
a: On narrowband (phone) audio the missing >6 kHz band removes a key genuine-speech cue, which pushes scores upward and inflates false positives if we kept 0.70. Raising HIGH to 0.85 (and MED to 0.55) compensates for that channel-induced score shift, trading some recall for precision so we do not flag legitimate phone customers. The narrowband flag changes only thresholds, never the stacker weights.

q: Trace the streaming 3 s window / 1 s hop design and its latency implication.
a: stream_analyze uses a 3.0 s window with 1.0 s hop, scoring each window with the same clip detector and maintaining running = mean(last 3 windows), plus a fast-flag if any single window ≥ 0.85. With a 1 s hop and 3-window mean, you need ~3 windows before the running mean is meaningful, which is why time-to-flag is ~3.0 s (all 5 test clips flagged at ≥3 s, within the 10 s target). Shorter hops would flag sooner but add compute; longer windows smooth more but delay.

q: Why average the last 3 windows instead of flagging on a single window score?
a: Mean-of-3 evidence accumulation suppresses transient single-window noise (a momentary artifact or a brief genuine anomaly) so a flag reflects sustained evidence, reducing false alarms on live audio. We keep a fast-flag escape hatch: any single window ≥ 0.85 flags immediately, so a very confident spoof is not delayed by averaging. This is a classic sensitivity/latency vs stability trade — the mean adds ~2 windows of latency for robustness.

q: The clip detector caps at 6 s but streaming covers the whole call. How does the localize/streaming path reuse the clip detector, and what is the honest limitation?
a: Streaming and partial-fake localization reuse the SAME clip detector, just applied to sliding 3 s windows across the full call rather than a single 6 s slice. This is honest reuse, not a separate temporal model: there is no dedicated sequence model that reasons across windows beyond the mean-of-3. So localization resolution is window-limited (3 s / 1 s hop) and inherits every weakness of the clip detector, including the benign-DSP evasion gap.

q: The /api/live-call SSE path uses 2.5 s window / 1 s hop while stream_analyze uses 3.0 s. Why the discrepancy?
a: The live-call SSE endpoint trades a slightly shorter 2.5 s window for lower time-to-first-score in an interactive call setting, at the cost of marginally noisier per-window estimates, whereas stream_analyze's 3.0 s window favors stability. Both keep a 1.0 s hop. It is a deliberate latency-vs-stability tuning per use case, not an inconsistency.

q: Justify the ~3.0 s time-to-flag against real fraud-call dynamics.
a: Latency trace shows all 5 clips flag at ≥3 s and within the 10 s target, GPU sub-second and CPU 3–8 s end-to-end. Three seconds is fast enough to intervene early in a scam call (which typically run minutes) while giving the mean-of-3 accumulator enough evidence to avoid false alarms. The honest caveat is n=5 streaming clips is a tiny sample, so the 3.0 s figure is indicative, not a tight SLA.

q: Why does pitch-shift +2 semitones devastate your detector (+48.8 pts to 56.3% EER) while Opus codec improves it?
a: Pitch shifting warps the spectral envelope and HF structure the detector keys on without being in the training distribution, so genuine and fake distributions collapse together — EER jumps to 56.3%, essentially chance. Opus improves (2.5%, −5.0 pts) because our training was codec-hardened, so Opus-coded audio is in-distribution and its compression even removes some confounding channel variance. The asymmetry is entirely about what augmentation the deployed model saw: codecs yes, benign pitch/tempo/noise no.

q: Rank your robustness degradations and state which is the single biggest security gap.
a: From robustness.json (n=80/cond, thr 0.70): pitch +2st 56.3% (+48.8), noise@15dB 45.0% (+37.5), tempo 0.9× 32.5% (+25.0), MP3 16k 20.0% (+12.5), G.711 8k 15.0% (+7.5), clean 7.5%, Opus 12k 2.5% (−5.0). The single biggest gap is benign-DSP evasion: an attacker needs no ML — just pitch/tempo/noise manipulation — to push us toward chance, so closing this via matched augmentation is the top roadmap item.

q: What is FGSM vs PGD, and where does VoxShield stand on white-box adversarial robustness?
a: FGSM perturbs the input one step along sign(∇ₓ loss) to cross the decision boundary; PGD iterates that projected onto an ε-ball for a stronger attack. VoxShield has NOT hardened against these — white-box adversarial (FGSM/PGD) defense is explicitly stated roadmap, not covered today. Our current robustness testing is benign DSP transforms, not gradient-based attacks, and I would not claim adversarial robustness we have not measured.

q: If benign pitch/tempo edits already break you, why bother worrying about gradient-based adversarial attacks?
a: Precisely because the benign gap is worse and cheaper to exploit — an attacker gets near-chance evasion with a one-line librosa pitch shift, no model access or gradients needed. Gradient attacks (FGSM/PGD) are the more sophisticated, lower-priority threat; the pragmatic security posture is to first close the benign-DSP hole via matched augmentation, then address white-box robustness. Claiming adversarial hardening while benign DSP defeats us would be dishonest.

q: Describe your replay/liveness defense and its threat model.
a: Liveness is a challenge-response: the system issues a random digit challenge, Silero VAD gates real speech into Whisper (base.en → tiny.en fallback, max_new_tokens=32), and we check the spoken digits plus response timing. This defeats replay of pre-recorded audio because the attacker cannot know the fresh challenge, and defeats silence/hallucination attacks via the VAD gate. It does not defeat a real-time interactive voice clone that can synthesize the challenged digits on demand — that is where the spoof stack and ECAPA must catch it.

q: State VoxShield's threat model explicitly — what it defends and what it concedes.
a: Defends: pre-recorded TTS/vocoder deepfakes on wideband and codec-degraded channels (EER 5.9%, codec-hardened), replay via liveness challenge, and enrolled-speaker impersonation via ECAPA. Concedes: benign-DSP-evaded spoofs (pitch/tempo/noise, +25 to +49 pts), white-box FGSM/PGD attacks (roadmap), real-time interactive clones that can answer liveness challenges, and any attack exploiting the open unauthenticated API. It is a TRL-5 validated detector, not a hardened production security product.

q: Explain FastAPI async here: what actually runs concurrently versus what is serialized?
a: FastAPI's event loop stays responsive because blocking ML work is offloaded via run_in_threadpool, and within a request the five detectors run concurrently in a ThreadPoolExecutor. Concurrency across the ML calls is real only to the extent the underlying ops release the GIL (torch/numpy native code does). Python-level work is serialized by the GIL, and model loading is serialized by _LOAD_LOCK to avoid an MPS init race — so 'concurrent' here means overlapped native compute, not true parallel Python.

q: If Python has a GIL, how do five detectors in a ThreadPoolExecutor give any speedup?
a: The GIL is released during native/C extension execution — torch tensor ops, numpy, and the SSL forward passes spend most time in native code with the GIL released, so multiple threads genuinely overlap that compute. The Python glue around them is serialized, but that is a small fraction of wall time. This is why threads (not processes) suffice: the heavy lifting is native, and threads avoid the serialization cost of pickling models across processes.

q: You run a single uvicorn process with no --workers. What are the throughput consequences?
a: A single process means one event loop and one GIL; concurrent requests share the same ThreadPoolExecutor and CPU, so throughput is bounded by CPU cores and native-op overlap, not by request parallelism. Under a POST flood (simulate_load.py) latency rises rather than the system scaling out. Horizontal scale (multi-worker / multiple replicas behind a balancer) is explicitly roadmap; today it is deliberately single-process for demo simplicity and auto-restarts on OOM.

q: There is no GPU batching and one clip is processed at a time. How would you add batching without breaking the API contract?
a: Today each request runs its own forward pass on CPU, one clip at a time — no device placement, no batch dimension. To batch I would introduce a micro-batching queue (e.g., collect requests for ~20–50 ms, pad/stack to a batch, run one GPU forward, scatter results) behind the same endpoint so the external contract is unchanged. That requires a GPU, a queue, and a batch scheduler — none exist today (they are roadmap: GPU batching + containerized queue).

q: All state is in-memory (AUDIT, _ENROLLED, ACTIONS, ...). What breaks at scale and how would you fix it?
a: In-memory state is lost on restart and not shared across workers, so multi-worker deployment would fragment enrollment, audit, blacklist and ring data per process — verification could pass on one worker and fail on another. The audit list is capped at 200 (returns 50), not persisted, and the SHA-256 hash is truncated to 16 hex (64-bit), so it is demo-grade, not tamper-evident. The fix is a shared datastore (DB + cache) for enrollment/audit/blacklist — explicitly roadmap; no database exists yet.

q: The audit hash is SHA-256 truncated to 64 bits. What is the security implication?
a: Truncating to 16 hex chars (64 bits) drops collision resistance from 2^128 to roughly 2^32 by the birthday bound, so it is a demo integrity fingerprint, not a cryptographic tamper-proof audit. Combined with the audit being an in-memory list (capped 200, returns 50, not persisted, not immutable), the audit trail is non-durable and non-authoritative. Immutable/persisted audit is explicitly slideware — we do not claim it as real.

q: The API has no auth, no CORS, no rate-limiting, no RBAC. Why is that acceptable for a fraud product, and what is the plan?
a: It is NOT acceptable for production — it is acceptable only for a TRL-5 demo where the box is not exposed to hostile traffic. The honest table marks JWT/OAuth/API-keys, rate-limiting, RBAC, CORS and AES-256-at-rest as slideware with no code. The roadmap explicitly lists adding auth (API keys/JWT), rate-limiting, CORS and real persistence. Presenting these as shipped would be a misrepresentation; they are targets.

q: The WebSocket only relays WebRTC signaling. Where does the audio actually flow and why does that matter?
a: The /ws/call/{room} WebSocket carries only WebRTC signaling (SDP/ICE); the media is peer-to-peer between browsers and never transits our server. This matters for privacy and bandwidth — we do not store or proxy raw call audio in the P2P path — but it also means server-side detection in that mode depends on whatever audio a client chooses to submit to /analyze, so the server is not a mandatory in-line tap for the WebRTC calls.

q: How is per-language false-positive rate measured and why is Telugu (13.3%) your weakest?
a: Per-language clean FP is measured on genuine Indic speech per language (30 clips each): Marathi 0.0, Tamil/Punjabi/Bengali 3.3, Kannada/Gujarati/Assamese 6.7, Hindi/Malayalam 10.0, Telugu 13.3. Telugu is weakest because English-trained SSL detectors misread its phonetics/prosody as anomalous, raising false alarms. With only 30 clips per language, 13.3% is 4/30 — small-n, so we present it as an honest weakest-case, not a precise rate.

q: Why do English-trained deepfake models misread genuine Indic speech as fake?
a: The SSL backbones and their deepfake heads were trained predominantly on English/Western speech, so genuine Indic phonetics, prosody (F0 contours, rhythm) and formant patterns fall outside their 'genuine' distribution and get scored as anomalous/synthetic. This is a distribution-shift false-positive problem, not a real spoof — which is why naive thresholds gave 11.7% Indic FP. We address it with channel-aware thresholds (→6.3%) and language-ID routing to an Indic-specific stacker.

q: Explain the Indic routing pipeline and its fallback.
a: Whisper-base does language-ID; if the language is Indic, we switch to an Indic-aware stacker (meta_fusion_indic.json, weights [0.617, −1.226, 1.600, 0.820, 1.156]) instead of the default stacker. If language-ID is unavailable/uncertain, a heuristic fallback fires when hf_energy_ratio < 0.0015. This routing raised Indic fake recall from 42% to 82% while leaving English EER unchanged at 5.9%, because it only redirects Indic-detected audio.

q: The Indic stacker weights differ from the default. Interpret weight 1.600 (XLS-R) being the largest.
a: In the Indic stacker [0.617, −1.226, 1.600, 0.820, 1.156], XLS-R gets the largest positive weight (1.600) versus 1.21 in the default, because XLS-R is the multilingual (128-language) model and is the most reliable detector on Indic speech — so the Indic-tuned fusion leans harder on it. Deepfake-V2 stays inverted (−1.226), consistent with its below-random behavior, while DistilHuBERT's weight drops (0.820 vs 2.22) since its English-centric confidence is less trustworthy on Indic audio.

q: Channel-aware thresholding cut Indic FP from 11.7% to 6.3%. Why does that help without retraining any model?
a: The Indic false positives were partly driven by channel/band characteristics pushing genuine scores up, so detecting the channel and raising the flag threshold (narrowband HIGH 0.85) removes those spurious flags without touching the detectors. It is a post-hoc decision-boundary fix, cheap and reversible: 11.7% → 6.3% Indic clean FP. It complements, and is separate from, the routing that fixes recall — thresholds fix false positives, routing fixes false negatives.

q: Indic fake recall went 42% → 82%. Why is 82%, not higher, and what artifact backs it?
a: exp_indicfull_result.json reports indic_fake_recall 0.823 (from live_indic_recall 0.417), so routing roughly doubled recall but still misses ~18% of Indic fakes because the detectors remain English-centric and only re-weighted, not retrained on Indic spoofs. We deliberately cite 42→82% routed and do NOT claim the '100% Indic fine-tune recall' from the deck, because that has no committed artifact — the fine-tuned XLS-R+AASIST Indic head is a local, undeployed roadmap asset.

q: With only 30 clips per language and n=320 held-out overall, how can you defend any fairness claim statistically?
a: We cannot make tight per-language claims — a 13.3% Telugu FP is 4/30 with a wide confidence interval (roughly ±12 pts at 95%), so we present per-language numbers as directional evidence of a real, reproducible disparity, not precise rates. The defensible claims are the aggregate shifts (Indic clean FP 11.7%→6.3%, fake recall 42%→82%) measured over larger pooled sets. Honest small-n reporting means flagging these as indicative and prioritizing more Indic data collection on the roadmap.

q: Describe your held-out evaluation protocol and how leakage is controlled.
a: The headline metrics are on held-out In-the-Wild data with n_train=480 and a disjoint n_test=320 split; the SSL backbones are frozen so no test audio ever updates them, and only the 5-weight stacker + calibration are fit on the training split. Because the base models are frozen and the split is disjoint, the main leakage risk is limited to the stacker/calibration seeing training statistics (μ, sd, Platt), which stay out of the 320-clip test. The per-detector 800-clip numbers are reported separately and clearly labeled.

q: Why does freezing the SSL models strengthen your leakage argument?
a: Because a frozen backbone cannot memorize or adapt to any evaluation audio — it is a fixed feature extractor — the only trainable parameters are the six stacker coefficients plus Platt {a,b} and the standardization μ/sd, all fit on the disjoint 480-clip train split. So the 320-clip test EER of 5.9% reflects generalization of a tiny linear head, not fine-tuned memorization. The remaining diligence is ensuring train/test clips come from disjoint sources, which the In-the-Wild split enforces.

q: Your per-detector table uses 800 clips but the fusion metric uses 320. Why the different denominators, and is that a fair comparison?
a: The per-detector EERs (XLS-R 16.0%, etc.) are reproduced from meta_scores.csv over the full 800-clip corpus to characterize each base model, while the fusion headline (5.9%) is on the disjoint 320-clip held-out test to avoid crediting the stacker for data it was fit on. They are different denominators by design, so one should compare fusion-vs-best-single at matched splits when making the 'stacking wins' claim; we are transparent that the 800-clip and 320-clip numbers are not the same evaluation set.

q: Source attribution claims to name the generator (ElevenLabs/Tacotron/In-the-Wild). How strong is that, really?
a: It is a genuinely-implemented but simple 3-class multinomial-softmax logistic model over the same 89-dim vector, firing when the top class score ≥ 0.5. It is linear, trained on limited classes, so it is a coarse, honest attribution — useful as a hint, not a forensic identification. We explicitly frame it as 'real but simple 3-class linear', not a robust generator fingerprinting system.

q: Derive the multinomial softmax used by source attribution and contrast it with the binary stacker.
a: For K=3 classes, p_k = e^(w_k·x + b_k) / Σ_j e^(w_j·x + b_j); the predicted class is argmax_k p_k, fired when max p_k ≥ 0.5. Unlike the binary stacker (one sigmoid, spoof-vs-genuine), this has one weight vector per class over the 89-dim input and normalizes across classes so probabilities sum to 1. It is trained with categorical cross-entropy rather than binary log-loss, but is still just a linear model — hence 'simple'.

q: Partial-fake localization: how does it work and what resolution can it actually claim?
a: Localization reuses the clip detector on sliding windows (the same 3 s / 1 s hop streaming machinery) and reports which windows score as fake, so a partially-spliced clip shows elevated windows. Its resolution is therefore bounded by the window/hop (≈3 s window, 1 s step), and it inherits every clip-detector weakness including benign-DSP evasion. It is honest windowed reuse, not a dedicated boundary-detection or segmentation model.

q: Digital Arrest Shield tracks scam stages Authority→Threat→Isolation→Extraction. What is real versus aspirational there?
a: Real in code today: scam-intent detection plus a stage tracker over those four stages, supporting English/Hindi/Hinglish, driven by the multilingual scam ASR (openai-whisper 'small', since 'base' mis-decodes Hindi→Urdu), and a citizen warning to call 1930. What is aspirational is any hardened, large-scale deployment guarantee; the feature itself is implemented but validated at TRL-5 scale, not proven on live IVR traffic (that pilot is roadmap TRL-6).

q: Why does Whisper 'base' mis-decode Hindi as Urdu, and why does 'small' fix it for scam ASR?
a: Hindi and Urdu are near-identical in spoken form (Hindustani) differing mainly in script and register, so a smaller Whisper with weaker language priors ('base') often labels Hindi audio as Urdu. The larger 'small' model has stronger acoustic-linguistic discrimination and gets the language/transcript right more often, which is why multilingual scam ASR uses 'small' despite the extra cost. It is a capacity-vs-latency trade specific to the Hindi/Urdu ambiguity.

q: Fraud-ring linkage is listed as real. Conceptually, how could it work given no database?
a: It links calls/entities by shared signals (e.g., matching voice embeddings, blacklisted identifiers) using in-memory structures like BLACKLIST and _RING. Because there is no database, the linkage graph lives only in process memory, is lost on restart, and is not shared across workers — so it is a working demo of the analytic, not a durable intelligence store. Persisting and sharing the ring graph is part of the same 'real persistence' roadmap item.

q: Walk the complete request path for /analyze from bytes to verdict.
a: Multipart UploadFile → load_audio resamples to 16 kHz mono, drops silence (top_db=30), caps first 6 s → compute 89-dim feature bank → run 5 detectors concurrently in a ThreadPoolExecutor (SSL pipelines lazy-loaded, serialized by _LOAD_LOCK) → standardize and apply logistic meta-stacker (weights above, b=0.134) → Platt calibration {6.446,−3.151} → apply channel-aware threshold (wideband 0.70/0.40 or narrowband 0.85/0.55) → emit verdict + reason codes (closed-form SHAP) + truncated SHA-256 audit entry. HIGH triggers human step-up, never auto-block.

q: Why lazy-load the three HF models and serialize with _LOAD_LOCK rather than eager-loading all at startup?
a: Lazy loading defers the memory cost until a detector is first needed and keeps cold-start light; _LOAD_LOCK serializes concurrent first-loads so two requests don't race to initialize the same model (which on Apple MPS could trigger an init race/crash). We do run a warmup on startup in a daemon thread to pre-pay the first-hit latency. The Docker image also bakes the models into HF_HOME so there is no runtime download.

q: The Dockerfile uses CPU torch and bakes 4 models but not ECAPA/LID/xlsr_antispoof. What are the deployment consequences?
a: The image (python:3.10-slim, CPU torch, EXPOSE 7860) bakes the 3 deepfake classifiers + whisper-base.en into HF_HOME so those work offline with no runtime download. ECAPA speaker verification, the Whisper language-ID model, and the 1.18 GB xlsr_antispoof are NOT baked, so speaker verification and Indic-LID routing would need to download on first use or are simply unavailable in that container. The fine-tuned xlsr_antispoof is gitignored and roadmap-only, so it never ships.

q: Backend is 2.2 GB and artifacts 1.2 GB (mostly xlsr_antispoof). How does that shape your deployment targets?
a: The 1.2 GB artifacts are dominated by the local-only xlsr_antispoof, so the deployable footprint is really the ~2.2 GB backend plus baked models. That fits the documented free/cheap CPU targets: HuggingFace Spaces (Docker CPU free), Render/Railway/Fly (Docker CPU paid), Mac+ngrok for demos, and a Vultr VPS via systemd+Caddy. Because we ship CPU torch, no GPU host is required — consistent with 'no GPU batching' today.

q: The VPS deploy adds 4 GB swap if RAM<6GB. Why is that a red flag for production and acceptable for a demo?
a: Relying on swap means the working set exceeds RAM, so ML inference pages to disk and latency becomes erratic — fine for a single-user demo box, unacceptable under concurrent production load where the single process would thrash. The systemd service runs at 127.0.0.1:8000 with Restart=always behind Caddy (:80 plain HTTP, HTTPS only if the operator edits the Caddyfile). It is an honest low-cost demo deployment, not a sized production cluster.

q: Caddy serves plain :80 HTTP by default here. What is the security exposure?
a: Plain HTTP means call audio and verdicts traverse the network unencrypted unless the operator manually enables HTTPS in the Caddyfile, and combined with no auth/CORS/rate-limiting the endpoint is fully open. TLS 1.3 pinning and AES-256-at-rest are slideware, not implemented. For a fraud product this is a clear gap; the honest posture is that transport security and auth are operator-configured/roadmap, and the default is a demo-grade open box.

q: How would you evolve this single-process app into a horizontally-scaled service without changing detection quality?
a: Externalize all in-memory state (AUDIT, _ENROLLED, ACTIONS, BLACKLIST, ROOMS, _RING) into a shared DB + cache; put multiple uvicorn workers/replicas behind a load balancer; add a GPU micro-batching inference service with a queue so forward passes batch across requests; and keep the frozen stacker/calibration identical so scores are byte-for-byte reproducible. None of this changes the model math — it changes serving. All of it is explicitly roadmap (multi-worker, GPU batching, containerized queue, DB, auth), so I would not claim it as built.

q: simulate_load.py floods concurrent multipart POSTs. What do you expect to observe and what does it prove?
a: Under a concurrent POST flood a single-process, CPU-only server shows rising latency and eventually queueing/OOM (mitigated by auto-restart), because request parallelism is bounded by cores and native-op overlap, not by workers. It proves the system stays correct under load and reveals the throughput ceiling — it does not prove horizontal scalability, which does not exist yet. It is an honest stress tool, useful for capacity-planning the roadmap scale-out.

q: Give the intuition for why a learned stacker's negative weights are strictly more expressive than any convex combination (voting/averaging).
a: Voting/averaging are convex combinations: weights are non-negative and sum to 1, so they can only interpolate between detector outputs and can never subtract an anti-correlated detector's signal. A logistic stacker places no such constraint — weights can be negative (Deepfake-V2 −1.17, DSP −0.55) and unbounded, plus a bias, so it spans a strictly larger function class. That extra expressiveness is exactly what lets it invert the below-0.5-AUC detector and reach 5.9% where averaging stalls at 19.1%.

q: How do reason codes get generated, and why are they trustworthy rather than post-hoc rationalizations?
a: Reason codes come directly from the closed-form SHAP φᵢ=(wᵢ/sdᵢ)(xᵢ−μᵢ), which are the exact additive contributions of each detector/feature to the final logit (Σφᵢ = final_logit − base_logit). Because they are computed from the actual model coefficients, not a separate explainer model, they are faithful by construction — the explanation is the decision, decomposed. That is stronger than a post-hoc surrogate that could disagree with the real model.

q: Could an attacker use your own SHAP reason codes to craft an evasion? How do you mitigate that?
a: In principle yes — since φᵢ=(wᵢ/sdᵢ)(xᵢ−μᵢ) exposes which detectors drive the score, an attacker who sees explanations learns which features to manipulate (e.g., pitch/tempo to fool the DSP-sensitive and HF cues). Mitigation is to keep reason codes internal to analysts (the API is currently open, which is itself a gap) and to close the benign-DSP hole via augmentation so the exploitable features become robust. This is why interpretability and the open-API/robustness gaps are linked risks.

q: What is the decision when max(distilhubert, xlsr) is high but the LFCC/CQCC head disagrees (<0.5)? Trace the gate.
a: The recall-floor gate requires BOTH max(distilhubert, xlsr) ≥ 0.90 AND the LFCC/CQCC head ≥ 0.5 to floor the score to ≥ 0.70. If the head is < 0.5, the gate does NOT fire, so the normal calibrated stacker output stands and could fall below the flag line. This two-condition design prevents a single overconfident SSL detector from forcing a flag — it demands corroboration from the independent 89-dim head.

q: Why might jitter/shimmer be unreliable clone cues on real telephony, and how does that interact with your robustness gap?
a: pyin F0 estimation degrades on band-limited, noisy telephony, so f0_jitter and shimmer become noisy — and any added noise (noise@15dB pushes EER to 45.0%) or pitch/tempo edit directly corrupts these prosodic scalars. So the same benign-DSP transforms that break us also happen to corrupt the prosody features, compounding the gap. This is why the DSP heuristic weights breath/prosody modestly and why matched augmentation (training with these corruptions) is the planned fix.

q: Your ECE is 0.044 with only ~320 test points. How reliable is that calibration estimate?
a: With n=320 spread across confidence bins, each bin holds only tens of points, so the per-bin accuracy estimate is noisy and the ECE (0.044) carries meaningful sampling error — differences of ~0.01 (versus the 0.031 uncalibrated) are within noise. That is precisely why we report both numbers and decline to claim calibration improved things. A trustworthy calibration claim would need a larger held-out set; small-n honesty applies to ECE just as to the per-language FP rates.

q: If a fraudster records a genuine customer and replays it (not a clone), which layer catches it and which does not?
a: The 5-detector spoof stack would likely NOT flag it — the audio is genuine, so there are no synthesis artifacts to detect; that is the wrong tool. The liveness challenge-response catches it, because the replayed recording cannot answer a fresh random digit challenge (VAD-gated Whisper checks the response). ECAPA would VERIFY the identity (it is the real voice), so replay defense rests specifically on liveness, not on spoof detection or speaker verification.

q: Explain why min t-DCF (0.252) and EER (5.9%) can move differently, and which you would optimize for banking.
a: EER fixes FAR=FRR symmetrically, while min t-DCF weights errors by their tandem-system costs and priors, so a threshold that minimizes t-DCF need not sit at EER — improving one can worsen the other depending on the cost asymmetry. For banking fraud, where a missed clone (false accept) can drain an account, I would optimize toward the t-DCF cost structure (and the recall-floor gate reflects that asymmetry), while still reporting EER for comparability with ASVspoof literature.

q: Summarize the single most important honest limitation you would state first to a technical judge, and your evidence-backed mitigation.
a: The top limitation is benign-DSP evasion: an attacker with no ML skill can pitch-shift (+48.8 pts → 56.3% EER), add noise (+37.5 → 45.0%) or time-stretch (+25.0 → 32.5%) genuine-looking spoofs to near chance, because the deployed model was codec-hardened but NOT augmented for pitch/tempo/noise. The evidenced mitigation is matched augmentation plus deploying the local fine-tuned XLS-R+AASIST Indic head (1.2 GB, currently gitignored/undeployed) — a concrete roadmap item, not a claimed capability. Everything else (single-process, no auth/DB, small n=320/30-per-language, simple 3-class attribution) I would disclose as demo-grade TRL-5 scope.
